title: [Vantage Point] Boardroom gymnastics, retail stakes: Unpacking the Rockwell deal
summary: FPH owes investors proof that nearly P16 billion in cash beats keeping a profitable property arm, just as Rockwell’s minorities deserve full clarity before deciding whether to stay put or cash out

blocks.text: Too often, financial reporting treats corporate dealmaking like a spectator sport for billionaires — fixating on which tycoon is buying control, which conglomerate is cashing out, and how much changes hands at the top.
Lost in the noise is what these corporate intramurals mean for the thousands of ordinary public investors whose capital sustains market valuations.
First Philippine Holdings’ (FPH) proposed sale of its controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Crème Investment Corporation for nearly P16 billion is a textbook case.

Strip away the prominent surnames, and two practical questions remain for everyday shareholders on both sides: Are FPH investors getting fair value for surrendering a profitable business, and will Rockwell’s minorities get enough hard facts to make an informed choice?

Signed on November 13, the deal carries an amended 11-month closing deadline measured from signing, down from 12 months, and awaits Philippine Competition Commission approval plus a mandatory tender offer for Rockwell’s remaining public shares. A signed agreement is only the opening act, not a finished sale.

For small investors reading the fine print, the headline numbers require unpacking. The P15.916-billion price tag covers P15.888 billion for 5.296 billion common shares at P3 apiece, plus P27.5 million for 2.75 billion preferred shares at P0.01 each.

While headlines highlight a 90.74% combined stake, measuring FPH’s common shares against Rockwell’s 6.117 billion outstanding common shares puts its common equity holding at roughly 86.58%. The combined percentage includes preferred stock; it is not the common-share stake being sold.

Equally crucial is where the money goes. Upon closing, the P15.916 billion gross consideration goes to FPH, not Rockwell. Because this is a secondary sale of existing stock rather than a capital raise, Rockwell receives zero fresh cash to build towers, pay down debt, or fund dividends. Minorities weighing whether to stay invested must recognize that the sale itself adds no cash to Rockwell’s balance sheet.
On the FPH side, small shareholders must temper expectations. Dividing P15.916 billion by FPH’s 424.5 million outstanding common shares equates to roughly P37.49 per share.
That merely measures deal scale — not a guaranteed special dividend or an automatic share-price jump. Taxes, transaction fees, and carrying value will ultimately dictate what hits the bottom line.

FPH did take visible steps to validate the P3 sale price. Adviser BDO Capital & Investment Corporation valued Rockwell’s common shares between P2.47 and P3.09 — putting the price near the top of the range — while independent directors, external counsel, and buyer adviser AlphaPrimus Advisors were brought in.

Yet governance checklists cannot replace transparent math. Public investors deserve to see how that valuation treated project spending, borrowing costs, cash collections, and recurring commercial income — and whether it included a control premium rather than pricing the block like an illiquid minority stake.

Rockwell’s latest results make this scrutiny even more urgent. FPH is not unloading a troubled unit: nine-month revenue climbed to P19.317 billion from P14.996 billion a year earlier, lifting profit attributable to parent shareholders by roughly 21.5% to P3.788 billion from P3.117 billion.

Though third-quarter attributable profit dipped about 10.7% to P1.076 billion from P1.205 billion — as nine-month non-operating expenses rose to P2.389 billion from P1.359 billion — one softer quarter hardly invalidates Rockwell’s long-term case.

At P3 per share, the deal values Rockwell at roughly 3.4 times trailing 12-month earnings of P0.88 per share. On paper, 3.4 times looks like a bargain for the buyer. While property accounting profits depend heavily on construction progress, revenue recognition, and financing costs — meaning net income rarely equals free cash — management must explain why such a modest multiple is fair to sellers.

Broker commentary underscores this tug-of-war between instant cash and lost income. Online trading platform COL Financial noted that the P15.9-billion consideration represents a 99% premium over its estimated net asset value for FPH’s Rockwell stake, raising its fair-value estimate for FPH by 11.8%. Yet COL also estimated that Rockwell accounts for roughly 25% of FPH’s net income. Unlocking asset value today leaves a sizable earnings hole tomorrow.

FPH says the proceeds will fund energy, infrastructure, and other growth ventures. Rotating capital out of mature assets makes sense, provided retail investors are told the recurring profits sacrificed, net cash left after costs, and expected returns from replacement projects — with any disposal gain reported separately from core earnings.

Meanwhile, Rockwell’s small shareholders face a pivotal choice once formal tender documents arrive. Beyond payment timelines and funding certainty, they must scrutinize the buyer’s plans. The tender price and complete terms still require confirmation. A change in control does not automatically trigger delisting, but tender acceptances could reduce public ownership below the PSE’s 10% minimum. Rockwell’s reported free float was 13.05% before the announcement. Anyone staying invested must weigh potential shifts in governance, debt appetite, and trading liquidity.

Finally, FPH’s disclosure that certain directors of the seller and buyer are related within the fourth civil degree raises the bar for accountability. Family ties do not prove wrongdoing, but detailing independent board vetting and director abstentions is essential if small investors are to trust the process.

Rockwell’s change-in-control filing left the buyer’s material relationships and directors’ transaction interests marked “to follow.” Those disclosures need completion before minorities decide whether to tender.

Public markets thrive only when everyday shareholders are treated as true stakeholders rather than passive bystanders to boardroom deals. FPH owes investors proof that nearly P16 billion in cash beats keeping a profitable property arm, just as Rockwell’s minorities deserve full clarity before deciding whether to stay put or cash out.

This analysis draws from FPH’s November 16 amended transaction disclosure, Rockwell’s ownership disclosure, its September 2026 quarterly financial report, and COL Financial’s November 13 research note. Ownership percentages, per-share proceeds, earnings growth, and the earnings multiple are our calculations; COL’s valuation and contribution estimates remain explicitly attributed.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com
